B11_00: A change in extracellular salt concentration forces cells to defend their volume and internal ion balance. An aldo-keto reductase generates sorbitol as a compatible osmolyte, an aquaporin provides regulated water flux, a potassium-chloride cotransporter and a sodium pump regulatory subunit tune ion movement, and a mechanosensitive cation channel reports swelling. Mitochondrial calcium uptake components link ionic stress to organelle homeostasis, while transcript-stability and DNA-repair factors handle hypertonic damage.
B11_01: Accumulating nitric oxide and peroxynitrite S-nitrosylate and tyrosine-nitrate proteins and damage DNA, and several arms of adaptation follow. A redox-sensitive protein acts protectively, a J-domain co-chaperone supports modified and misfolded proteins, autophagic turnover clears damaged cargo, an apical checkpoint kinase couples nitrosative DNA lesions to arrest signalling, and a stress-induced leucine zipper factor links persistent stress to apoptotic commitment, placing the response between proteostasis and genome surveillance.
B11_02: Hydroperoxides generated by lipid oxidation are sensed and answered with changes in gene expression, redox enzyme output, survival signalling or growth arrest. A scavenger receptor delivers oxidised lipid cargo that adds to the oxidant load, membrane-associated glutathione transferase activity supplies detoxification, and oxidation-resistance and p53-induced stress genes bias the outcome toward antioxidant defence or death. Two kinases transduce the oxidant signal and corepressor activity links it to transcriptional reprogramming.
B11_03: Permanent exit from the division cycle is held off by several mechanisms. A reverse transcriptase with its RNA template extends chromosome ends and a telomere-binding protein caps them, so the ends are not read as damage; two NAD-dependent deacetylases restrain damage and stress responses at chromatin. Transcriptional repressors suppress the kinase-inhibitor arrest programme, a cyclin-dependent kinase and other cycle regulators sustain proliferation, and microRNAs damp arrest-promoting transcripts.
B11_04: Oxidative or genotoxic insult can impose an irreversible exit from the division cycle. A stress-activated MAP kinase and its downstream kinase relay the signal to p53, which induces a cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor that locks cells out of S phase. Modifiers set the threshold: an NAD-dependent deacetylase restrains p53 activity, a secreted WNT ligand contributes to the paracrine phenotype, and a circadian transcription factor links the response to metabolic rhythms.
B11_05: Leucine availability is monitored and licenses anabolism. When it is abundant, sestrins release a pentameric regulatory complex, and a tRNA synthetase and small GTPases allow the growth kinase complex to dock on the lysosomal surface; withdrawal reverses this, so kinase activity falls, protein synthesis and ribosome biogenesis are curtailed, and autophagy is de-repressed to recover amino acids. Uncharged tRNA accumulation also drives a transcriptional arm inducing transporters and synthetases.
B11_06: Oxygen above normal tension drives reactive species production, with NADPH oxidase activity adding superoxide to the burden, and cells answer with stress signalling, clearance and eventual death. A forkhead transcription factor redirects gene expression toward stress resistance and apoptosis, death receptor signalling commits irreversibly damaged cells to apoptosis, and autophagy requiring a conjugating enzyme clears oxidised proteins and damaged mitochondria. A membrane scaffold protein links the membrane to these decisions.
B11_07: Cells exposed to a higher external solute concentration lose water and shrink, and two arms restore volume. A kinase cascade in which WNK kinases activate two STE20-family kinases switches on cation-chloride cotransport to reaccumulate ions, while a tonicity-responsive transcription factor drives expression of organic osmolyte machinery, including the reductase that makes sorbitol, so volume is regained without raising intracellular ionic strength. Aquaporin water flux and cytoskeletal remodelling accompany it.
B11_08: Low oxygen primes mitochondria to release apoptogenic factors, and several mechanisms block that route. Survival signalling through phosphoinositide and MAP kinase cascades sustains anti-apoptotic gene expression, an apoptosis repressor with a caspase recruitment domain blocks caspase activation, a stress-inducible endoplasmic reticulum chaperone and a transmembrane BAX inhibitor buffer calcium release and outer membrane permeabilisation, and a mitochondrial kinase preserves organelle quality control. Glycolytic adaptation supports survival.
B11_09: Hydrogen peroxide is both a metabolic by-product and a deliberate second messenger, and the response ranges from restored redox balance to arrest and regulated death. Catalase, thioredoxin and a redox-sensitive protein limit the signal, a cap-n-collar transcription factor drives the antioxidant programme. Peroxide-sensitive kinases relay the stimulus, an NF-kappaB subunit links it to cytokine transcription, and cation channels convert it into calcium signals.
B11_10: Falling energy charge activates a heterotrimeric AMP-sensing kinase, which restrains anabolic signalling and licenses autophagy via a class III phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase complex. In parallel, the kinase arm of the unfolded protein response drives a bZIP factor that induces amino-acid supply enzymes, while sestrins, a forkhead factor, p53 and a deacetylase reinforce catabolic and antioxidant programmes. Nutrient transporters and lipid droplet coat proteins tie sensing to internal fuel mobilisation.
B11_11: These inputs amplify the response to falling oxygen, making the programme stronger or longer-lasting than the oxygen signal alone would produce. The contributing activities are heterogeneous rather than a single complex: a de novo DNA methyltransferase links the stimulus to epigenetic reprogramming, a two-pore potassium channel and a metabotropic glutamate receptor connect membrane excitability and transmitter signalling to oxygen stress, and two microRNAs tune the downstream transcript pool.
B11_12: Several inputs push cells into permanent cycle exit. A damage-activated transcription factor sits at the centre, supported by effector genes it induces and by cytosolic DNA sensing, which reads displaced chromatin fragments and adds an interferon-flavoured arrest signal. MicroRNAs reinforce the decision by silencing proliferative and survival transcripts, and an NAD-dependent deacetylase tunes the central factor's response. The output is durable growth arrest with altered secretion.
B11_13: Cells in a dilute medium take up water and swell, and the response restores volume. Detection begins with membrane stretch sensed by a stretch-activated cation channel and by water flux through aquaporins; solutes then leave through chloride channel and potassium-chloride cotransport pathways, driving regulatory volume decrease. Two WNK-activated kinases with their scaffold set cotransporter phosphorylation according to tonicity, while myosin light chain kinase links volume change to cytoskeletal tension.
B11_14: Several mechanisms keep peroxide-stressed cells alive. Survival signalling from a receptor tyrosine kinase converges on a serine-threonine kinase that suppresses apoptotic commitment, while a scaffold protein and a mitochondrial chaperone restrain death machinery at the organelle. Two mitochondrially protective proteins limit oxidative damage and support removal of damaged mitochondria. Several microRNAs tune the same survival programmes post-transcriptionally, and a carbonic anhydrase contributes antioxidant thiol buffering.
B11_15: How readily peroxide permeabilises mitochondria and commits a cell to caspase activation is tuned by a mostly inhibitory set of factors. Kinase signalling promotes survival, two mitochondrial protective proteins limit oxidative damage, and a mitochondrial chaperone restrains permeabilisation. A scaffold protein organises the kinases involved, a carbonic anhydrase contributes antioxidant thiol capacity, and two microRNAs add post-transcriptional control, placing the decision between redox buffering and the mitochondrial apoptotic arm.
B11_16: These inputs push accumulating peroxide toward death rather than detoxification, increasing the rate and extent of programmed cell death. A stress-responsive forkhead transcription factor drives pro-apoptotic and redox target genes, a pro-apoptotic effector partner reinforces the response, and a mitochondrial nuclease is released to fragment nuclear DNA in a caspase-independent branch. A microRNA and a forkhead-family repressor add post-transcriptional and transcriptional tuning, so sensitivity is set by gene expression.
B11_17: Falling zinc availability is answered by remodelling transport and transcription, because many enzymes and transcription factors require the ion as a cofactor. Two members of a zinc transporter family mediate uptake and transcellular handling, adjusting acquisition at the membrane. Downstream, a zinc-finger transcription factor and an immediate-early factor alter target gene output, including secreted matrix proteins and a surface receptor, so that the most zinc-dependent functions are preserved.
B11_18: A change in external osmolarity is converted into a corrective response. Mechanosensitive and osmotically gated cation channels provide an entry point for calcium, while a WNK-STE20 kinase module couples tonicity to phosphorylation of cation-chloride cotransporters and so to ion and water movement. Hypotonic and hypertonic stress also converge on an inflammasome with its adaptor and caspase, linking volume disturbance to interleukin processing.
B11_19: Strong, sustained signalling through a small GTPase pathway can impose permanent proliferative arrest instead of transformation. Arrest is enforced by cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitors, nuclear bodies built on a scaffold protein organise the associated signalling, and architectural HMG-box proteins help remodel chromatin into heterochromatic foci that lock down proliferative genes. A lineage transcription factor connects the state to broader transcriptional reprogramming, and the cells become flattened and secretory.
B11_20: Output of the lipogenic transcription factors is controlled mainly at the precursor's escape from the endoplasmic reticulum. Two membrane proteins retain the cleavage-activating complex in the ER when sterols are abundant, blocking transport to the Golgi where proteases release the active factor, while scaffolding and trafficking proteins influence complex assembly. Further restraint follows activation, with ubiquitin ligases promoting turnover of the mature nuclear form and microRNA inputs tuning component levels.
